intro: A cor anglais sings over muted strings in the New World Symphony’s Largo. Dvořák surrounds that simple tune with wandering wind chords, a C♯-minor lament and a return so quiet that the string sections shrink to solo players.

sections.label: A · Wind chords find D♭
sections.mNote: Low winds and brass move from E major to D♭

sections.label: B · Cor anglais over muted strings
sections.mNote: The solo song begins above softly held chords

sections.label: C · Flutes and oboes in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: A minor-key tune leads to a measured plucked bass

sections.label: D · A quick oboe figure
sections.mNote: The oboe starts a dance in C♯ major

sections.label: E · The first movement breaks in
sections.mNote: Brass recalls earlier tunes against the Largo’s melody

sections.label: B′ · The cor anglais returns
sections.mNote: The song returns over four players in each upper string part

sections.label: A′ · Wind chords, then double basses
sections.mNote: The opening chords return before the divided basses finish alone

relations.label: The cor anglais song returns
relations.basis: The large A–B–A′ design restores the opening song after the central minor-key and climactic passages. The later excerpt begins at the return marked near 520 s, not at an inferred instrument entrance. CENS diagonal mean 0.927, sustained 27.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 482.5 s (cache/form/dvorak-9-largo.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Chords before the song
cues.text: Clarinets, bassoons and brass begin with a solemn chain of chords. E major is their starting point; D♭ major is where they land. The violins enter muted, and the wind choir leaves the stage to a single cor anglais.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 73, bars 1–7. The chord sequence is set out in the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four notes make a song
cues.text: The cor anglais begins with just four pitches: F, A♭, E♭ and D♭. Its dotted rhythm gently lifts each phrase above the muted strings. The tune has scarcely any notes, and all the time it needs.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, movement II, bars 7–10: the opening solo uses those four sounding pitches. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clarinet tune becomes cor anglais
cues.text: In the sketches Dvořák gave the melody to a clarinet, in a more European shape. In the score it passes to the cor anglais, with a stronger pentatonic outline. The instrument’s tone is said to have reminded him of the singer Harry T. Burleigh’s voice.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, Symphony No. 9, discussion of the Largo: the original clarinet scoring, the altered melody and the association with Burleigh’s voice. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: “The Legend Begins”
cues.text: Two phrases are written into Dvořák’s sketches for this movement: “Legend” and “The Legend Begins”. Michael Beckerman hears the opening chords as a musical “once upon a time”. The sketchbooks hold earlier versions of them, one beginning and ending in C major.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, Symphony No. 9: the sketchbook inscriptions, the surviving variants of the opening chords and Beckerman’s reading. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Fisher writes “Goin’ Home”
cues.text: In the summer of 1922, Dvořák’s former pupil William Arms Fisher plays a piano arrangement of the Largo. Words begin coming to him. He turns the cor anglais melody into the song Goin’ Home, nearly thirty years after the symphony.
cues.evidence: Fisher’s account of composing the words in summer 1922 is quoted in the performance-history section of the work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: “It is a lie!”
cues.text: In February 1900 Dvořák sends Oskar Nedbal, who is preparing to conduct the symphony in Berlin, a published analysis of it. He asks him to leave out “that nonsense about my using Indian and American motifs – it is a lie!” He had meant only to write in the spirit of American national melodies.
cues.evidence: Dvořák to Oskar Nedbal, February 1900, in the English translation given in the Dvořák work catalogue, “sources of inspiration”: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: The same note, in minor
cues.text: D♭ becomes C♯: the same sounding tonic, now in minor. Flutes and oboes share a more restless tune over repeated string chords. Later, plucked bass notes give this middle section the tread of a funeral march.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 78, Un poco più mosso, and the ensuing pizzicato passage. The minor section and march are described in the Dvořák work catalogue.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Indian melodies from a friend
cues.text: Dvořák told the New York Herald in December 1893 that he had “carefully studied a certain number of Indian melodies which a friend gave me”. Iroquois performers sang and danced in Prague for ten days in August 1879. He saw Buffalo Bill’s Wild West show only in spring 1894, after the symphony was done.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, “sources of inspiration”: the New York Herald interview of 15 December 1893, the Iroquois visit to Prague in August 1879, and David Beveridge’s 2022 research on the date of the Buffalo Bill visit. https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: A queue in the rain
cues.text: On 15 December 1893, people queue in heavy rain for the public rehearsal at Carnegie Hall. Every seat sells. Anton Seidl conducts the New York Philharmonic; the official première follows the next evening.
cues.evidence: The première section of the Dvořák work catalogue describes the rain, queue, sold-out public rehearsal and concert: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: The oboe starts dancing
cues.text: A quick solo oboe figure breaks the long phrases into little groups of notes. Flutes and clarinets join it with trills and runs. C♯ major brightens the harmony, and the strings begin to swell beneath the dance.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 84, rehearsal 4: solo oboe, then flute and clarinet figures above a string crescendo. The C♯-major episode is identified in the work catalogue.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The whole symphony interrupts
cues.text: The little dance grows into an orchestral outburst. Themes from the first movement return beside the Largo’s own melody, with the brass projecting above the strings. The cor anglais song has acquired some formidable company.
cues.evidence: The work catalogue identifies the Largo theme, the first movement’s main theme and its closing theme in this climax: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/. Šourek score, printed pp. 85–88.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cor anglais comes home
cues.text: Meno mosso, Tempo I: the first pace returns. The cor anglais sings again in D♭ major, over just four players in each violin, viola and cello part. The tune is surrounded by much less sound than before.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 88, rehearsal 5: returning cor anglais, five-flat signature and four players in each upper string part.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two players, then one
cues.text: The string parts shrink again: two players in each, then solo violin, viola, cello and bass. Pauses separate the phrases. A whole symphony orchestra has become a handful of people playing very softly.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 89, bars 105–110: two players per string part, fermatas and subsequent solo markings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Applause after the Largo
cues.text: At the première on 16 December 1893, Dvořák’s son Otakar remembered in his memoirs, the audience would not let the concert go on after the Largo until his father appeared to bow. Otakar was in the hall.
cues.evidence: Otakar Dvořák’s memoirs, quoted in the première section of the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: The wind chords return
cues.text: Bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba bring back the introductory chords. Their slow steps lead to D♭ major once more. After the last wind chord, divided double basses carry the music down into silence.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 91–92, bars 120–127: return of the wind chords and final divided double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The winds leave one voice
transitions.to: B · Cor anglais over muted strings
transitions.how: The wind chords travel from E major to D♭. Their final G♭-minor chord resolves onto D♭ major, a minor-subdominant plagal cadence. Muted strings take over the held harmony, and the cor anglais begins its tune above them. The double basses settle on D♭.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 73, bars 1–7; the chord succession is given at https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

transitions.title: D♭ turns into C♯ minor
transitions.from: B · Cor anglais over muted strings
transitions.to: C · Flutes and oboes in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The song subsides, and D♭ is respelt C♯. E♮ replaces F as the third above it, turning the harmony to minor. At Un poco più mosso, flutes and oboes take the new tune together over repeated second-violin and viola chords.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 77–78, leading into bar 46, Un poco più mosso.

transitions.title: The oboe quickens the phrase
transitions.from: C · Flutes and oboes in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The minor-key strings soften onto a held C♯. A solo oboe starts a quick figure above them; flutes and clarinets answer with trills and running notes. The tonic stays C♯, but the major third E♯ brightens this small dance.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 84, rehearsal 4. The work catalogue identifies the episode as a quasi-scherzo in C♯ major.

transitions.title: The brass brings back earlier tunes
transitions.to: E · The first movement breaks in
transitions.how: The strings swell beneath the quick wind figures. Brass and timpani join the growing orchestra, and themes from the first movement sound against the Largo tune. The short dance has expanded into a meeting of three melodies.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 85–88. The combination of the Largo melody with the first movement’s main and closing themes is described in the Dvořák work catalogue.

transitions.title: Four strings to a part
transitions.from: E · The first movement breaks in
transitions.how: The orchestra slows and softens into Meno mosso, Tempo I. The cor anglais recovers the D♭-major song over four players in each upper string part. Brass and timpani make their last quiet punctuation, then leave the melody to the cor anglais and strings.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed p. 88, rehearsal 5: original tempo, D♭-major return and reduced string numbers.

transitions.title: The wind choir returns
transitions.to: A′ · Wind chords, then double basses
transitions.how: The solo violin’s last phrase dwindles to ppp. Bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba recover the opening chord sequence, moving once more towards D♭ major. The bass gives each chord its own footing; the final withdrawal belongs to divided double basses.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 91–92, the return of the introductory chords at bar 120 and final bass writing.

source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, II. Largo, full score (Otakar Šourek edition)
source.locator: Printed pp. 73–92, bars 1–127: cor anglais over muted strings, the C♯-minor middle, quick wind figures and reduced strings at the return. The tuba plays in the opening and closing chords; its rests are confirmed in the Breitkopf part, https://www.imslp.eu/files/imglnks/euimg/5/59/IMSLP726228-PMLP8710-Dvorak-Symph9-29-ta.pdf.

timeline.note: Clarinets, bassoons and brass move through solemn chords; timpani mark the arrival in D♭ before muted strings enter.
The cor anglais sings above muted strings; clarinet figures move gently beneath the later phrases.
Woodwind phrases swell into a brief brass chord before the strings resume the song.
First violins take the melody, then pass it back to the cor anglais above quietly held strings.
Flutes and oboes sing together in C♯ minor above repeated second-violin and viola chords.
Oboe and clarinet answer the violins, while plucked low strings give the lament its measured tread.
Short woodwind phrases remain above the quiet strings as the C♯-minor lament subsides.
A quick solo oboe figure passes to flutes and clarinets, with the strings swelling beneath their trills and runs.
Brass recalls the first movement’s tunes against the Largo melody, with timpani beneath the full strings and winds.
The cor anglais returns over four players in each violin, viola and cello part.
The strings shrink to two players in each part, then to solos, with pauses between the phrases.
Bassoons, horns, trombones and tuba recover the opening chords; the strings rise towards the last cadence.
The last wind chord dies away, leaving divided double basses to finish alone.

composer.epithet: He had played viola in the opera pit for nine years before the world discovered the composer of the Slavonic Dances.
facts: Violist at Prague’s Provisional Theatre, 1862–71; organist and piano teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of New York’s National Conservatory, 1892–95
Nine symphonies; operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs
composer.background:
In the village band at Nelahozeves, north of Prague, the musicians collected their money by stopping a couple halfway through a dance and asking them to pay. Young Antonín Dvořák handed his share straight to his father, the village butcher and innkeeper. “I belonged to ours as soon as I could fiddle a little,” he told the London Sunday Times on 10 May 1885. He had been born there on 8 September 1841.

At Zlonice, the schoolteacher Antonín Liehmann taught him harmony and several instruments. Dvořák remembered bringing home a polka for the band to try: the opening chord came out all right, except for the cornet, whose part he had written in the wrong key. In 1857 he went to the Prague Organ School, graduating two years later. He played viola in a dance band which became the nucleus of the Provisional Theatre orchestra in 1862. For nine years he sat in the pit, often under Smetana, playing operas while writing his own music at home.
